topics: Antenatal Care: Focused ANC, Danger Signs and Screening
Labour and Delivery: Stages of Labour, Partograph and Active Management of Third Stage
Postpartum Care: Uterine Involution, Lochia, Breastfeeding and Family Planning
Obstetric Emergencies: Shoulder Dystocia, Cord Prolapse, Obstructed Labour and Uterine Rupture

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of focused antenatal care?

choices.text: To provide care only when complications develop
To promote maternal and fetal health through preventive, promotive and clinical interventions
To prepare pregnant women exclusively for hospital delivery
To reduce the number of antenatal visits for all pregnant women

questions.rationale: Antenatal care aims to promote maternal and fetal well-being through early identification of risks, preventive interventions, health education and appropriate management. It also supports birth preparedness, complication readiness and timely referral.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attends her first antenatal clinic at a district hospital at 10 weeks of gestation. Which intervention is particularly important during this initial visit?

choices.text: Performing an immediate elective caesarean section
Conducting a comprehensive baseline assessment, including medical history, blood pressure, blood group and relevant laboratory investigations
Waiting until the third trimester before performing any investigations

questions.rationale: The first antenatal contact provides an opportunity to establish baseline maternal health and identify pre-existing conditions or pregnancy-related risks. Investigations commonly include haemoglobin assessment, blood grouping and Rh status, HIV and syphilis screening, and hepatitis B screening according to national protocols.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a danger sign during pregnancy that requires immediate medical assessment?
questions.rationale: Vaginal bleeding during pregnancy may indicate serious complications such as miscarriage, placenta praevia or placental abruption. Immediate assessment is necessary to determine the cause and initiate appropriate management.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation visits a CHPS compound complaining of severe headache, blurred vision and swelling of her face. What should the community health nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Severe headache and visual disturbances are warning features of pre-eclampsia, particularly after 20 weeks of gestation. The nurse should assess blood pressure, arrange urgent referral and avoid delaying evaluation for proteinuria or other investigations.

questions.question_text: Which supplement is routinely recommended during pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects in the developing fetus?
questions.rationale: Folic acid is essential for normal neural tube development and helps prevent neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Supplementation should begin before conception where possible and continue during early pregnancy.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks of gestation reports that she has not felt fetal movements throughout the day, although fetal movements were previously regular. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Reassure her that reduced fetal movement is always normal
Advise her to return after one week
Arrange immediate assessment of fetal well-being

questions.rationale: Reduced or absent fetal movements may indicate fetal compromise and require prompt assessment. Fetal heart activity and other appropriate investigations should be undertaken without unnecessary delay.

questions.question_text: Which investigation is most appropriate for screening a pregnant woman for anaemia during antenatal care?
questions.rationale: Haemoglobin estimation helps identify anaemia during pregnancy and guides appropriate management. Anaemia increases the risk of maternal complications and may reduce the mother's ability to tolerate blood loss during childbirth.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attending antenatal clinic has a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL. She complains of fatigue, dizziness and palpitations. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

choices.text: Reassure her that the findings are normal in pregnancy
Assess the severity and possible cause of anaemia and arrange appropriate clinical management
Advise her to stop taking all prescribed supplements

questions.rationale: A haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL indicates moderate anaemia in pregnancy and requires clinical assessment and treatment. Management may include therapeutic iron and folic acid, investigation of the underlying cause and referral depending on clinical condition and national protocols.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the purpose of birth preparedness and complication readiness?

choices.text: To encourage pregnant women to deliver without skilled assistance
To help the woman and family plan for childbirth and respond effectively to obstetric emergencies
To eliminate the need for antenatal attendance

questions.rationale: Birth preparedness and complication readiness involve planning the place of delivery, skilled birth attendance, transport, financial arrangements and emergency contacts. These measures reduce delays in accessing appropriate obstetric care.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation attends a CHPS compound with vaginal bleeding but no abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination immediately
Advise her to remain at home and observe the bleeding
Arrange urgent referral to a hospital and avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded
Encourage her to walk to reduce the bleeding

questions.rationale: Painless vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy raises suspicion of placenta praevia, although other causes must be considered. Digital vaginal examination may provoke severe haemorrhage if placenta praevia is present and should be avoided until placental location is established.

questions.question_text: Which event marks the beginning of the first stage of labour?

choices.text: Onset of regular painful uterine contractions accompanied by progressive cervical dilatation and effacement

questions.rationale: The first stage of labour begins with the onset of labour characterised by regular uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change. It ends when the cervix is fully dilated at approximately 10 cm.

questions.question_text: A woman in active labour is admitted to a district hospital. Her cervix is 6 cm dilated, and uterine contractions are regular. Which assessment is particularly important for monitoring labour progress?

choices.text: Monitoring cervical dilatation, fetal heart rate and uterine contractions

questions.rationale: Monitoring cervical dilatation, fetal heart rate and uterine contractions provides important information about labour progress and fetal well-being. Maternal observations and the overall clinical condition must also be monitored and documented.

questions.question_text: The second stage of labour begins when:

choices.text: The cervix becomes fully dilated and ends with delivery of the baby
The placenta separates from the uterine wall

questions.rationale: The second stage begins at full cervical dilatation and continues until the complete birth of the baby. During this stage, fetal descent and expulsion occur through coordinated uterine contractions and maternal bearing-down efforts.

questions.question_text: A midwife is monitoring a woman in labour using a partograph. Which parameter is primarily used to assess the progress of cervical dilatation?
questions.rationale: The partograph or appropriate labour-care monitoring tool records cervical dilatation in relation to time alongside other maternal and fetal observations. It supports recognition of abnormal labour progress and timely clinical decision-making.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a fetal heart rate of 100 beats per minute on repeated assessment. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Recognise possible fetal bradycardia, urgently assess the clinical situation and initiate appropriate corrective measures
Encourage the woman to push immediately regardless of cervical dilatation
Administer oral food and discharge the woman

questions.rationale: A persistent fetal heart rate below 110 beats per minute is abnormal and may indicate fetal compromise. The midwife should urgently assess for reversible causes, escalate care and prepare for expedited birth if indicated.

questions.question_text: Which intervention is a key component of active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL)?

choices.text: Routine administration of a prophylactic uterotonic after birth
Routine manual removal of the placenta in every woman
Routine fundal pressure to expel the placenta
Withholding uterotonic medication until severe bleeding develops

questions.rationale: Administration of a prophylactic uterotonic, commonly oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly or intravenously according to protocol, is a central component of AMTSL. Controlled cord traction by a trained birth attendant and assessment of uterine tone are also included in appropriate third-stage management.

questions.question_text: Immediately after delivery of the baby, a midwife administers oxytocin as part of active management of the third stage of labour. What is the main purpose?

choices.text: To prevent postpartum haemorrhage by promoting uterine contraction

questions.rationale: Oxytocin stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction, helping compress maternal blood vessels at the placental site. This reduces the risk of uterine atony and postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.question_text: A woman in the second stage of labour has a fully dilated cervix and the fetal head is visible at the perineum. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Provide supportive care, monitor fetal well-being and assist controlled delivery of the head
Ask the woman to stop breathing throughout the second stage
Leave the woman unattended until the baby is delivered

questions.rationale: The midwife should provide continuous support, monitor maternal and fetal condition and facilitate controlled birth. Appropriate perineal support and communication help reduce preventable birth trauma.

questions.question_text: A partograph shows that cervical dilatation is progressing poorly, and the woman has increasingly strong contractions. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.text: The labour is progressing normally in all circumstances
There may be abnormal labour progress requiring reassessment and evaluation for the cause
The woman should immediately be discharged
The findings confirm normal fetal oxygenation

questions.rationale: Poor cervical progress despite strong contractions may indicate labour dystocia, including possible cephalopelvic disproportion or malposition. The midwife should reassess the mother and fetus, evaluate the cause and escalate care according to the clinical findings rather than relying on the chart alone.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has been pushing for a prolonged period, and the fetal head is not descending despite adequate contractions. Which condition should the midwife investigate?
questions.rationale: Failure of fetal descent despite adequate uterine contractions raises concern about obstructed labour. Potential causes include cephalopelvic disproportion, malpresentation and malposition, and urgent obstetric assessment is required.

questions.question_text: What is uterine involution?

choices.text: The progressive return of the uterus towards its pre-pregnancy size after childbirth
The enlargement of the uterus during pregnancy
The separation of the placenta during labour
The development of breast milk during pregnancy

questions.rationale: Uterine involution is the process through which the enlarged uterus gradually returns towards its pre-pregnancy size and condition after delivery. It involves myometrial contraction and cellular changes and is assessed through uterine fundal examination.

questions.question_text: A woman on her second day after vaginal delivery has a firm uterus and moderate red vaginal discharge. Which type of lochia is she most likely experiencing?
questions.rationale: Lochia rubra is the initial postpartum vaginal discharge, usually red and containing blood, decidual tissue and mucus. It is commonly observed during the first few days after childbirth.

questions.question_text: Which hormone is primarily responsible for milk production in the mammary glands?
questions.rationale: Prolactin stimulates milk synthesis in the alveolar cells of the mammary glands. Suckling stimulates prolactin secretion and supports continued breast milk production.

questions.question_text: A mother who delivered 24 hours ago complains that her newborn is not feeding effectively. Which intervention should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Advise the mother to stop breastfeeding
Assess positioning and attachment and assist with effective breastfeeding
Recommend giving water before every breastfeed
Separate the mother and baby for several days

questions.rationale: Effective positioning and attachment are essential for successful breastfeeding and adequate milk transfer. Early breastfeeding support also helps prevent nipple trauma and encourages exclusive breastfeeding.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes exclusive breastfeeding?

choices.text: Giving breast milk together with water from birth
Giving only breast milk, with no other food or drink except prescribed medicines, vitamin or mineral supplements and oral rehydration solution when indicated
Giving breast milk and fruit juice during the first month
Giving breast milk only during the first two weeks

questions.rationale: Exclusive breastfeeding means providing only breast milk for the first six months, apart from prescribed medicines, vitamin or mineral supplements and oral rehydration solution when indicated. It provides appropriate nutrition and immune protection for the infant.

questions.question_text: A woman develops heavy vaginal bleeding shortly after delivery. On examination, her uterus is soft and poorly contracted. What is the most likely cause?
questions.rationale: Uterine atony occurs when the uterus fails to contract effectively after delivery, resulting in continued bleeding from placental site vessels. It is a major cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage and requires immediate management.

questions.question_text: A woman is breastfeeding her newborn and requests contraception before discharge from a district hospital. Which method is compatible with breastfeeding when appropriately selected and initiated?

choices.text: Combined hormonal contraception immediately after delivery in every woman
Emergency contraception as the only long-term family planning method

questions.rationale: Progestogen-only contraceptive methods are generally compatible with breastfeeding and may be initiated according to postpartum eligibility criteria. The choice should consider the woman's medical history, preferences, timing after delivery and current contraceptive guidelines.

questions.question_text: A woman on the fifth day after delivery reports foul-smelling vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain and fever. What condition should the midwife suspect?
questions.rationale: Fever, lower abdominal pain and foul-smelling lochia are concerning features of postpartum genital tract infection. Puerperal sepsis requires urgent clinical assessment, appropriate antimicrobial treatment and monitoring for systemic deterioration.

questions.question_text: A woman develops sudden heavy vaginal bleeding two hours after delivery. She is pale, restless and has a pulse rate of 128 beats per minute. What is the priority nursing action?

choices.text: Leave the patient to rest and reassess after one hour
Activate the obstetric emergency response, call for help and initiate immediate postpartum haemorrhage management
Discharge the patient because delivery has been completed

questions.rationale: Heavy bleeding accompanied by tachycardia, pallor and restlessness suggests postpartum haemorrhage with possible hypovolaemic shock. Immediate emergency response, uterine assessment, resuscitation, treatment of the cause and urgent escalation are essential.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the defining clinical feature of pre-eclampsia?

choices.text: Hypertension developing after 20 weeks of gestation with proteinuria and/or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction
Hypotension occurring before 12 weeks of gestation
Fever and vaginal bleeding during early pregnancy

questions.rationale: Pre-eclampsia is a multisystem hypertensive disorder that develops after 20 weeks of pregnancy and is characterised by new-onset hypertension with proteinuria or other maternal organ dysfunction. Proteinuria is not essential when other diagnostic features of pre-eclampsia are present.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks of gestation presents with a blood pressure of 170/115 mmHg, severe headache and visual disturbances. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.rationale: A systolic blood pressure of at least 160 mmHg or diastolic pressure of at least 110 mmHg represents severe-range hypertension in pregnancy. Severe headache and visual symptoms indicate possible neurological involvement and require urgent management.

questions.question_text: Which medication is primarily used to prevent and treat seizures in women with severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia?
questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is the recommended anticonvulsant for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures. It acts on the central nervous system to reduce neuromuscular excitability and must be administered with appropriate monitoring.

questions.question_text: A woman receiving magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia develops absent patellar reflexes, respiratory depression and reduced urine output. What should the midwife suspect?
questions.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and oliguria are important signs of magnesium sulfate toxicity. The infusion should be stopped, urgent clinical assistance obtained and calcium gluconate administered as the antidote according to protocol.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia suddenly develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the labour ward. What is the priority nursing action?

choices.text: Insert a spoon into her mouth to prevent tongue biting
Protect her from injury, maintain airway and breathing, call for emergency assistance and administer magnesium sulfate as prescribed
Give oral antihypertensive medication during the seizure

questions.rationale: Eclampsia is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate protection from injury and management of airway, breathing and circulation. Magnesium sulfate is used to control and prevent further seizures, while severe hypertension and the need for delivery are addressed by the obstetric team.

questions.question_text: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. Which assessment finding should alert the midwife to possible toxicity?

choices.text: Respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute
Urine output of 50 mL per hour
Consciousness and orientation within normal limits

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression is a serious manifestation of magnesium sulfate toxicity. Regular assessment of respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output is essential during magnesium sulfate therapy.

questions.question_text: Which definition best describes primary postpartum haemorrhage?

choices.text: Excessive blood loss occurring within 24 hours after childbirth
Blood loss occurring only during pregnancy
Normal vaginal discharge during the puerperium
Blood loss occurring exclusively after six weeks postpartum

questions.rationale: Primary postpartum haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours following childbirth. Contemporary clinical definitions recognise cumulative blood loss of at least 1000 mL or bleeding accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolaemia, while any significant bleeding requires prompt assessment.

questions.question_text: A woman develops postpartum haemorrhage following vaginal delivery. Her uterus is enlarged and boggy on palpation. Which intervention should the midwife perform immediately while activating emergency management?

choices.text: Perform uterine massage and assess uterine tone
Encourage the woman to walk around
Apply abdominal heat without further assessment

questions.rationale: A boggy uterus suggests uterine atony, a major cause of postpartum haemorrhage. Immediate uterine massage, uterotonic treatment, resuscitation and assessment for other causes should occur simultaneously through an organised emergency response.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is included in the recognised '4 Ts' framework for identifying causes of postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.rationale: The 4 Ts framework categorises postpartum haemorrhage causes as uterine Tone abnormalities, genital tract Trauma, retained placental Tissue and coagulation problems involving Thrombin. It helps guide systematic investigation and management of bleeding.

questions.question_text: A woman develops severe postpartum bleeding following delivery. Her blood pressure is falling, pulse is rapid and she appears confused. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Immediate resuscitation, activation of the haemorrhage protocol and urgent escalation
Waiting for laboratory results before initiating treatment

questions.rationale: Hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status suggest haemorrhagic shock, which can rapidly become fatal. Immediate resuscitation, intravenous access, blood sampling, appropriate fluid and blood replacement, uterotonic treatment and definitive control of bleeding are required.

questions.question_text: A woman experiences persistent postpartum haemorrhage despite uterine massage and administration of prescribed uterotonics. Examination suggests retained placental tissue. What is the most appropriate next action?

choices.text: Continue routine observation without further intervention
Arrange urgent obstetric assessment and appropriate management of retained placental tissue
Apply pressure to the woman's chest

questions.rationale: Retained placental tissue can prevent effective uterine contraction and cause persistent haemorrhage. Urgent obstetric assessment and appropriate removal or other definitive management are required alongside continued resuscitation and haemorrhage control.

questions.question_text: Which condition is characterised by failure of the fetal shoulders to deliver spontaneously after delivery of the head, requiring additional obstetric manoeuvres?
questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia occurs when the fetal shoulders fail to deliver spontaneously after the head has been born, commonly because the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal symphysis pubis. It is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate manoeuvres to facilitate birth.

questions.question_text: During vaginal delivery, the fetal head is born but retracts against the maternal perineum, producing the turtle sign. What should the midwife suspect?
questions.rationale: The turtle sign is a characteristic clinical indication of shoulder dystocia, in which the fetal head retracts against the perineum because the shoulders are impacted. Immediate assistance and appropriate shoulder dystocia manoeuvres are required.

questions.question_text: Which manoeuvre is recommended as the initial manoeuvre for managing shoulder dystocia?

choices.text: Internal podalic version in every case

questions.rationale: The McRoberts manoeuvre involves hyperflexion and abduction of the maternal hips towards the abdomen, helping alter pelvic dimensions and facilitate shoulder delivery. Suprapubic pressure may be used as an additional manoeuvre when indicated, while fundal pressure must be avoided.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour presents with sudden abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding and cessation of previously strong uterine contractions. The fetal presenting part is no longer well applied to the cervix, and fetal heart activity is abnormal. What should the midwife suspect?
questions.rationale: Sudden abdominal pain, abnormal fetal heart rate, loss of uterine activity and altered fetal station may indicate uterine rupture. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent operative intervention.

questions.question_text: A midwife discovers umbilical cord prolapse during labour, and the fetal heart rate falls to 80 beats per minute. What is the priority intervention while preparing for emergency birth?

choices.text: Attempt to push the cord back into the uterus
Relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part and position the woman appropriately while arranging emergency delivery
Ask the woman to begin pushing forcefully

questions.rationale: Umbilical cord prolapse can cause acute fetal hypoxia through compression of the cord between the presenting part and maternal pelvis. Immediate elevation of the presenting part, appropriate maternal positioning and expedited delivery, usually by emergency caesarean section when vaginal birth is not immediately achievable, are essential.

questions.question_text: A woman with prolonged labour develops severe abdominal pain, maternal tachycardia and signs of fetal distress. The uterus is tender, and the presenting part is abnormally high. Which condition is most likely?

choices.text: Obstructed labour with possible impending or established uterine rupture

questions.rationale: Prolonged obstructed labour can cause uterine exhaustion, maternal deterioration and uterine rupture. Severe abdominal pain, abnormal fetal findings and altered presenting-part station require immediate emergency obstetric assessment and intervention.

questions.question_text: A woman at a district hospital has been in labour for several hours with no cervical progress despite strong contractions. The fetal head remains high, and caput formation is increasing. What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Continue augmentation with oxytocin without reassessment
Suspect obstructed labour, stop inappropriate augmentation and arrange urgent obstetric review and referral or operative delivery
Encourage vigorous maternal pushing regardless of cervical dilatation
Discharge the woman to continue labour at home

questions.rationale: Failure of labour progress with a high presenting part and increasing caput suggests possible obstruction and cephalopelvic disproportion. Further oxytocin augmentation without excluding obstruction may increase the risk of uterine rupture and fetal compromise.

questions.question_text: Which statement best defines puerperal sepsis?

choices.text: A genital tract infection occurring during pregnancy only
A reproductive tract infection occurring during or after childbirth, associated with systemic illness
Normal bacterial colonisation of the vagina without illness
A condition characterised only by postpartum breast engorgement

questions.rationale: Puerperal sepsis refers to infection of the genital tract occurring during childbirth or the postpartum period, with potentially serious systemic consequences. Early recognition and appropriate antimicrobial treatment are essential to prevent maternal morbidity and mortality.

questions.question_text: A woman presents on the fourth day after caesarean section with fever, lower abdominal pain and foul-smelling lochia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Puerperal endometritis is an infection of the uterine lining that may present with fever, uterine tenderness and foul-smelling lochia. It is more common following caesarean delivery and requires prompt clinical assessment and antimicrobial treatment.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman has a temperature of 39°C, pulse rate of 130 beats per minute, hypotension and altered consciousness. What should the midwife prioritise?

choices.text: Immediate recognition of possible maternal sepsis, emergency escalation and initiation of the sepsis management protocol
Waiting until the following morning to repeat observations
Encouraging the woman to walk independently

questions.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension and altered consciousness suggest severe infection with possible septic shock. Immediate emergency management includes resuscitation, prompt appropriate antimicrobial therapy, investigations and source control.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes postpartum depression?

choices.text: A depressive disorder occurring after childbirth that may affect maternal functioning and bonding
A normal increase in maternal appetite
A condition characterised exclusively by postpartum vaginal bleeding
A brief emotional response that always resolves within 24 hours

questions.rationale: Postpartum depression is a clinically significant depressive disorder that may develop during the postpartum period. It can affect mood, sleep, appetite, maternal functioning and the relationship between mother and infant.

questions.question_text: A woman five days after delivery reports tearfulness, mood changes and emotional sensitivity but continues to care for her baby and has no thoughts of self-harm. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.rationale: Postpartum blues commonly occur during the first few days after delivery and may involve tearfulness, irritability and mood fluctuations. Symptoms are generally mild and resolve within approximately two weeks, but persistent or worsening symptoms require assessment for postpartum depression.

questions.question_text: A woman three weeks after delivery reports persistent sadness, loss of interest in activities, feelings of worthlessness and difficulty bonding with her baby. Which condition should the midwife suspect?
questions.rationale: Persistent depressive symptoms, loss of interest and feelings of worthlessness beyond the typical period of postpartum blues suggest postpartum depression. The woman requires comprehensive mental health assessment, including evaluation of suicide risk and possible risk to the infant.

questions.question_text: A woman ten days after delivery tells the midwife that voices are commanding her to harm her newborn and that the baby has been replaced by an evil spirit. What is the priority nursing action?

choices.text: Reassure her that these beliefs are normal after childbirth
Recognise possible postpartum psychosis, ensure immediate safety of mother and infant and arrange emergency psychiatric assessment
Advise her to sleep for several days without further assessment
Leave her alone with the infant to encourage bonding

questions.rationale: Hallucinations and delusions in the postpartum period strongly suggest postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency associated with substantial risk of harm. Immediate protection of the mother and infant, urgent specialist assessment and appropriate treatment are essential.

questions.question_text: A woman with postpartum depression expresses feelings of hopelessness and says she has been thinking about ending her life. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Tell her that motherhood should make her happy
Conduct an immediate suicide-risk assessment, maintain her safety and arrange urgent mental health intervention
Advise her to discontinue breastfeeding immediately
Recommend that she avoid discussing her feelings

questions.rationale: Suicidal thoughts indicate a potentially life-threatening mental health emergency and require immediate assessment and intervention. The midwife should ensure the woman is not left without appropriate support and arrange urgent specialist care.
